title: Workflow Before Hardware: The Three Phases of Testing
summary: Watch a faster analyzer fail to speed up a lab, find the real bottleneck across the three testing phases, and calculate what hand-sorting tubes really costs.

reviewer.note: Teaches the chapter’s core idea (workflow before technology), Hits 1–3, 6–7, Trap 1 and the Figure 2 memory anchor. Adds the error distribution across phases from an external review. The reviewer’s numeric examples (10 s per tube; 4 vs 10 tests per sample) are taught as the reviewer’s examples and kept as pending claims.

objectives: Name the three phases of the testing process and place an error in the right phase.
Explain why workflow analysis must come before buying technology.
Distinguish sample mapping (staffing) from test mapping (instrument capacity).
Calculate the daily labor cost of a manual step from time per tube and tube volume.

scenes.title: A faster analyzer — and nothing changed
scenes.altText: A lab installs a shiny new analyzer labelled “2× faster”. Specimen tubes keep piling up at a sorting bench before the analyzer, and a turnaround-time badge stays red: “still slow”. The cartoon scientist looks puzzled.

cues.text: This lab bought a new analyzer that runs twice as fast. Everyone expected results to come out sooner.
But tubes still pile up at the sorting bench, long before they reach the analyzer.
Turnaround time barely moved. How can a faster machine not make the lab faster?

scenes.title: Every test has three phases
scenes.altText: Three panels in a row: Preanalytical (order, collect, label, transport, sort), Analytical (measure on the instrument) and Postanalytical (verify, report, interpret). A tube slides from the first panel to the last. A bar of error shares then appears under the panels from one large study: about 62% preanalytical, 15% analytical, 23% postanalytical. Finally a token reads “Value = Quality ÷ Cost”.

cues.text: Every lab test travels through three phases. Think of them as before, during and after the measurement.
Preanalytical is everything before the analyzer: the order, the draw, the label, the trip to the lab, and sorting.
Analytical is the measurement itself. Postanalytical is checking the result, reporting it, and the clinician using it.
Where do errors happen? In one large study, about 62 percent were preanalytical, 23 percent postanalytical, and only 15 percent analytical. The analyzer is usually the strongest link.
The reviewer sums up the goal as Value equals Quality divided by Cost. You raise value by improving quality, lowering cost, or both. In health care, “quality” usually means patient outcomes.

scenes.title: Buying hardware first moves nothing
scenes.altText: The same three panels shrink to a strip. The analytical panel is upgraded (“2× faster”) but tubes stay piled in the preanalytical panel at sorting. Then a workflow-mapping toolbox appears with four tools: sample mapping (tubes arriving per hour → staffing), test mapping (tests per hour → instrument capacity), tube analysis and task mapping. Two bars compare a morning inpatient peak of about 4 tests per sample with an evening outpatient peak of about 10.

cues.text: Here is what went wrong. The new analyzer only sped up the analytical phase — the part that was already fast.
The tubes are still waiting at sorting, in the preanalytical phase. The bottleneck never moved.
So first, map the workflow. Sample mapping counts how many tubes arrive each hour. That tells you how many people you need, and when.
Test mapping counts how many tests are ordered each hour. That tells you how much instrument capacity you need. Tube analysis and task mapping follow each tube and each job.
The reviewer’s example: the morning inpatient peak has about 4 tests per tube, the evening outpatient peak about 10. Similar tubes, very different instrument load.

scenes.title: In the lab: what hand-sorting really costs
scenes.altText: A worked calculation. A stopwatch shows 10 seconds to sort one tube. The calculation 1,200 tubes × 10 s = 12,000 s; 12,000 ÷ 3,600 = 3.3 hours per day fills in step by step. Then tubes that went to three benches are routed to one consolidated workcell and the hours shrink. A final card reports a real microbiology laboratory that automated and applied Lean: samples per staff member per day rose from 49 to 110.

cues.text: Put a number on hands-on work. In the reviewer’s example, sorting one tube by hand takes about 10 seconds.
A lab sorts 1,200 tubes a day. 1,200 times 10 seconds is 12,000 seconds. Divide by 3,600 seconds in an hour: about 3.3 hours of labor, every single day.
If one tube’s tests can run on one consolidated workcell, the tube is sorted once instead of being split among benches. Those hours shrink.
A real example: one microbiology lab automated and then applied Lean. Samples per staff member per day rose from 49 to 110, and Lean added turnaround gains that automation alone did not deliver.

scenes.title: The trap: “just buy a new analyzer”
scenes.altText: A trap card “Old analyzers are the problem — buy new ones first” is stamped with a red cross and replaced by “Map the workflow first”. Two tokens pair sample mapping with staffing and test mapping with instruments. Then three error tokens drop into the right phase: mislabeled tube → preanalytical, calibration drift → analytical, late critical-value call → postanalytical.

cues.text: Classic trap: “Our analyzers are old, so step one is buying new ones.” That is wrong.
Step one is always workflow analysis: map samples, tests, tubes and tasks before spending money.
Don’t swap the maps: sample mapping guides staffing; test mapping guides instruments.
And place each error in its phase: a mislabeled tube is preanalytical, calibration drift is analytical, a critical value called late is postanalytical.

scenes.title: Map before you shop
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a road map unrolls first, then a shopping cart with an analyzer rolls in — “MAP before you SHOP”. A toll-booth picture shows a sports car stuck in the same queue as everyone else. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: MAP before you SHOP. Workflow first, hardware last.
Picture a traffic jam at a toll booth. A faster car still waits in the same line. Fix the booth, not the car.
Where it breaks: sometimes the instrument really is the bottleneck — it is broken, outdated, or too small for the volume. Mapping is how you find that out, too.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: A workflow map spans the three phases, with the analyzer drawn small in the middle and a check mark over the map.

cues.text: Map the whole workflow — preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical — before buying technology, because a faster analyzer cannot fix a bottleneck in sorting, transport or reporting.

explanation.what: Plain language: a lab test is a trip with three parts — before the machine, the machine, and after the machine. Making only the machine faster does not help if tubes are stuck somewhere else. Scientific terms: the total testing process has preanalytical (ordering, collection, labeling, transport, sorting and processing), analytical (measurement) and postanalytical (verification, reporting, interpretation) phases. Workflow analysis — sample mapping, test mapping, tube analysis and task mapping — finds where time, labor and errors actually build up.
explanation.why: Turnaround time is set by the slowest step, and in most labs that is not the analyzer. Published studies find most errors outside the analytical phase (one large study: about 62% preanalytical, 15% analytical, 23% postanalytical). A faster analyzer therefore only speeds up the step that was already strong. Value is often summarized as quality relative to cost, so spending money where it does not raise quality lowers value.
explanation.measure: Labs count tubes arriving per hour (sample mapping) to set staffing, count tests ordered per hour (test mapping) to size instruments, and time manual steps. Example: 1,200 tubes × 10 s = 12,000 s ≈ 3.3 hours of labor per day. Turnaround time and error rates per phase show whether a change helped.
explanation.differs: Preanalytical vs analytical vs postanalytical: before, during or after measurement. Sample mapping vs test mapping: tubes per hour (people) vs tests per hour (instruments). Workflow analysis vs technology purchase: analysis comes first; technology is a tool, not the fix.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “What should the lab do before buying a new analyzer?” (analyze and reengineer workflow), “Which phase has the most errors?” (preanalytical), sorting an error into its phase, a labor-time calculation, and Value = Quality ÷ Cost.

comparisons.title: Preanalytical vs analytical vs postanalytical
comparisons.distinguisher: Ask when the step happens: before, during, or after the measurement.

comparisons.title: Sample mapping vs test mapping
comparisons.distinguisher: Tubes need hands; tests need instrument time.

mnemonic.explanation: Map samples, tests, tubes and tasks first; buy technology only after you know where the bottleneck is. Like a toll-booth jam, a faster car (analyzer) still waits in the same line.
mnemonic.limitation: Sometimes the instrument really is the bottleneck — broken, obsolete or undersized — and must be replaced; mapping is how you prove that. The toll-booth picture also hides that errors, not just delays, concentrate outside the analytical phase.

analogyLimitations: The toll-booth comparison only covers delay, not errors or cost.
The piled-up tubes and three-bench layout are illustrative, not a real laboratory floor plan.
The 10-seconds-per-tube and 4-vs-10 tests-per-sample figures are the reviewer’s examples; real labs must measure their own.
takeaway: Map the whole workflow — preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical — before buying technology, because a faster analyzer cannot fix a bottleneck in sorting, transport or reporting.

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory has long turnaround times, and managers propose buying a faster chemistry analyzer. What should the laboratory do first?

options.text: Map the workflow — samples, tests, tubes and tasks — to find where delays occur
options.rationale: Correct. Technology alone does not improve performance; workflow analysis shows whether the analyzer is even the bottleneck.
Incorrect. If the delay is in sorting, transport or reporting, a faster analyzer only speeds up a step that was already fast.

options.text: Add staff only at the analyzer bench
options.rationale: Incorrect. Without mapping, the lab does not know where staff are needed; sample mapping guides staffing by hour.

options.text: Remove tests from the menu to lower volume
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cutting the menu does not identify the bottleneck and may harm patient care.

questions.stem: A processing area hand-sorts 900 tubes a day, and each tube takes 12 seconds. About how many hours of labor does sorting use per day?

options.rationale: Correct. 900 × 12 s = 10,800 s; 10,800 ÷ 3,600 s per hour = 3.0 hours.
Incorrect. 10,800 ÷ 60 = 180 gives minutes, not hours; divide by 3,600 to get hours.
Incorrect. This is off by a factor of ten — dividing by 36,000 instead of 3,600.
Incorrect. This treats an hour as 1,000 seconds; an hour is 3,600 seconds.

questions.stem: Which of these is a preanalytical error?

options.text: A tube labeled with the wrong patient’s name at the bedside
options.rationale: Correct. Labeling happens before measurement, so it is preanalytical — the phase with the most errors in published studies.

options.text: A calibration drift on the analyzer
options.rationale: Incorrect. Calibration problems occur during measurement, so they are analytical.

options.text: A critical potassium result phoned to the nurse two hours late
options.rationale: Incorrect. Reporting happens after measurement, so it is postanalytical.

options.text: A clinician misreading a correct result
options.rationale: Incorrect. Interpretation of a reported result is postanalytical.

claims.text: The total testing process has preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical phases; preanalytical covers ordering through specimen processing, postanalytical covers reporting and interpretation.
Most laboratory errors occur outside the analytical phase; one large study found about 62% preanalytical, 15% analytical and 23% postanalytical.
Laboratories should analyze and redesign current workflow before (or alongside) automation; automation alone does not deliver the full improvement.
In one microbiology laboratory, automation plus Lean raised productivity from 49 to 110 samples per FTE per day.
Value relates quality (outcomes) to cost; raising quality or lowering cost raises value.
claims.note: The reviewer’s formula Value = Quality ÷ Cost is a simplification; definitions of value in laboratory medicine vary by stakeholder.
Arithmetic is correct; the 10-seconds-per-tube input is the reviewer’s example and was not independently verified.

claims.text: Morning inpatient peak ≈ 4 tests per sample; evening outpatient peak ≈ 10 tests per sample.

accuracyFlags.resolution: Lesson presents the formula as the reviewer’s summary and notes that quality usually means outcomes.
